days.title: IAM Fundamentals
days.summary: Users, groups, roles and policies; identity vs resource policies with the real evaluation order — implicit deny by default, an explicit Allow grants, an explicit deny overrides every Allow, cross-account needs Allows on both sides; the six policy types, permissions boundaries, STS temporary credentials, MFA device kinds, Access Analyzer and key hygiene; monitoring with CloudTrail and credential reports. Summary, main concepts, flashcards, true/false and pop quizzes.

days.title: EC2 Compute Fundamentals
days.summary: What belongs on EC2, the four instance controls, launching and connecting (SSH, RDP, Session Manager), the instance lifecycle and status checks, and where EC2 sits on the compute spectrum; instance-type naming, AMI anatomy, user-data bootstrapping with IMDSv2, placement groups (7-per-AZ spread limit), tenancy and the 2024 public-IPv4 $0.005/hour change; plus VPC and load-balancing groundwork basics.

days.title: AWS Lambda Fundamentals
days.summary: Serverless: functions, the three invocation modes, memory-driven CPU (~1,769 MB per vCPU) and the 15-minute ceiling, request + GB-second billing with the permanent free tier, the hard quotas (memory 128 MB–10,240 MB, 6 MB sync / 1 MB async payloads, 4 KB env vars, 10 GB container images), async retries with on-failure destinations and dead-letter queues, reserved vs provisioned concurrency, runtimes/zip/container packaging, versions and aliases, execution roles vs resource policies, and Lambda vs EC2 on the compute spectrum.

days.title: S3 and Storage
days.summary: The EC2 storage trio (EBS vs EFS vs instance store), S3 object storage with 11-nines durability vs designed availability and strong read-after-write consistency, its seven storage classes with the fine print (30/90/180-day minimums, 128 KB minimum objects, per-GB retrieval fees) plus Intelligent-Tiering, versioning, lifecycle and CRR/SRR replication, Block Public Access, presigned URLs and the SSE options, the EBS deep dive (SSD vs HDD, gp2-vs-gp3 tuning, Multi-Attach, incremental snapshots), plus Storage Gateway, AWS Backup, FSx, EFS operating modes and Elastic Disaster Recovery, with clickable tier and type drills.

days.title: AWS Networking Fundamentals
days.summary: Amazon VPC from first principles: region-scoped isolation and your own CIDR, the three networking zones, subnets and tiers across AZs, route tables and the internet gateway, NAT gateways, stateful security groups (cross-group rule sources) vs stateless NACLs with the ephemeral-ports trap, the five reserved IPs and DHCP option sets, gateway vs interface (PrivateLink) VPC endpoints with per-AZ hourly billing, VPC Flow Logs, the two DNS switches, a hands-on two-tier custom VPC build, the inside-out troubleshooting checklist with VPC Reachability Analyzer, and where VPC peering, Transit Gateway and site-to-site VPN fit — with interactive pick-your-fix drills.

days.title: AWS Database Fundamentals
days.summary: Tables, attributes and tuples, primary and foreign keys; Amazon RDS with its five engines and 12-month free tier plus a hands-on EC2-to-RDS build, read replicas (read-scaling, promotable for DR) vs multi-AZ failover, and point-in-time backups vs manual snapshots; the NoSQL trio (key-value, document, graph) and DynamoDB with partition + sort keys, table classes and capacity modes plus the fine print (400 KB items, 4 KB/1 KB capacity units, Streams, Global Tables, DAX); the RDS-vs-DynamoDB comparison on schema, scaling, locking and cost; Amazon Aurora's cluster storage — six-way replication across three AZs, auto-growth to 128 TiB, writer/reader endpoints — and Serverless v2; migration with AWS DMS and SCT; and the in-memory pair, ElastiCache vs MemoryDB for Redis — with a pick-the-DB service-selection drill.

days.title: Understanding AWS Cost Drivers
days.summary: The five cost drivers — compute, storage, databases, data transfer, networking — and what each one's bill depends on; the pricing trio (free tier shapes, Reserved Instances and Savings Plans vs on-demand, plus Spot); Cost Explorer and Billing dashboards with cost-allocation tags, static thresholds and anomaly-detection alerts; the five provisioning decisions and right-sizing with Trusted Advisor and Compute Optimizer; manual vs auto scaling with spend caps; and the six classic overspending scenarios with their mitigations — with a pick-the-pricing-option drill. Plus a dedicated Cost Explorer quiz — the 12-month/18-month-forecast window story, grouping dimensions, the no-forecast-when-grouped rule, the hourly opt-in, 24-hour refresh and invoice-difference caveats, anomaly detection, RI/Savings-Plans utilization reports, recommendations and tag activation. And a separate AWS Budgets quiz — the six budget types, free monitoring (62 budget-days, then $0.02/day) with the first two action-enabled budgets free, IAM/SCP/EC2/RDS stop actions, the 8–12-hour refresh cadence against anomaly detection, and actual-vs-forecast thresholds plus the pre-created free-tier usage alert.

days.title: Understanding Amazon CloudFront
days.summary: Why a CDN exists — content close to the end user, with Amazon’s own research putting the cost at about 1% of sales per 100 ms of latency; CloudFront’s 2026 edge network as verified from AWS docs today — 750+ PoPs in 100+ cities across 50+ countries, 1,140+ embedded PoPs inside ISP networks and 15 regional edge caches; the full request flow: authoritative-DNS PoP selection, Host-header distribution mapping, cache behaviors matched by path pattern, then edge cache → regional edge cache → Origin Shield → origin; origins of every shape (S3, EC2, ALBs, API Gateway, MediaPackage, any HTTP server) with multiple origins, primary/secondary origin groups and private-subnet VPC origins; Origin Access Control over legacy OAI — the three signing behaviors, SigV4-signed requests and the cloudfront.amazonaws.com bucket policy with the distribution-ARN condition; distributions and the default catch-all behavior with the cache-key / origin-request / response-header policy trio; edge compute — CloudFront Functions (sub-millisecond, viewer events, millions req/s) vs Lambda@Edge (30 s, 10 GB memory on origin events, network and body access) vs the new Connection Functions inside the mTLS handshake; TTLs, invalidations and their in-progress limits; price classes; and 2026 pricing — pay-as-you-go with the 1 TB + 10M-requests + 2M-functions free tier, the new flat-rate plans (Free $0 · Pro $15 · Business $200 · Premium $1,000, no overage charges) and the up-to-30% Security Savings Bundle.

days.title: Week 2 Review
days.summary: Week 2 integrated on one interactive review page — the five sessions from Oct 26 to Oct 30: S3 and the storage family (EBS vs EFS vs instance store, seven storage classes with the 30/90/180-day minimums, 128 KB minimum objects and retrieval fees, versioning/lifecycle/CRR-SRR, Block Public Access, presigned URLs, SSE options, EBS gp3 tuning and incremental snapshots); Amazon VPC (subnets and tiers across AZs, route tables, IGW, NAT gateways, stateful security groups vs stateless NACLs with the ephemeral-ports trap, gateway vs interface endpoints and PrivateLink, the two DNS switches, five reserved IPs, Flow Logs, Reachability Analyzer, peering vs Transit Gateway vs VPN); databases (RDS's five engines, read replicas vs multi-AZ, point-in-time restore, DynamoDB keys/capacity/Streams/Global Tables/DAX with the 400 KB cap, Aurora's six-way cluster storage to 128 TiB and Serverless v2, DMS/SCT, ElastiCache vs MemoryDB); the five cost drivers with the pricing trio (Reserved Instances up to 72%, Savings Plans, Spot), Cost Explorer windows and Budgets actions; and CloudFront (750+ PoPs, 1,140+ embedded PoPs, 15 regional edge caches, the request flow, OAC's three signing behaviors, cache behaviors and the policy trio, CloudFront Functions vs Lambda@Edge vs 2026 Connection Functions, 2026 pricing). 27 concept cards, 40 flashcards, 40 true/false, and three quizzes — the last a week-wide name-the-service drill. Review page format mirrors a day page.

days.title: AWS Global Infrastructure and Deployment Context
days.summary: Week 3 opens with navigation and deployment context — exam-focused notes (CLF-C02 Domain 1) — the three infrastructure categories (Regions, Availability Zones, edge locations) with today’s live footprint verified from AWS (39 Regions / 124 AZs, minimum three AZs per Region, 2 more Regions announced, GovCloud US as two US-sovereign Regions); AZ names as account-relative labels vs AZ IDs that name the same physical location in every account (use1-az-style, the pin for cross-account zonal designs); Console and CloudShell as two views of the same region-bound context (default us-east-1, enabled regions only, sts get-caller-identity proving the shared identity, regional VPCs invisible across views); the four-box pre-deployment checklist (account, region, service, availability) applied to a public EC2 test web server launched end to end (test account for blast radius, us-west-2 for Pacific Northwest users, default VPC learning-only caveat, public IP, inbound-HTTP security-group rule, user-data bootstrap, no key pair); what a wrong-context deployment costs — vanished and duplicated resources, latency, data-residency violations, per-region pricing (t3.medium ~$0.042/h us-east-1 vs ~$0.067/h sa-east-1, on-demand Linux Shared, verified 2026-11-02) and metered cross-region and cross-AZ transfer; restoring the right context by AMI, volume snapshot or IaC redeploy; the five service families mapped to their scopes (compute regional, EBS zonal with mobile snapshots, S3 one-region placement under the global-namespace name rule plus the new opt-in account regional namespaces, VPC CIDR-overlap rule, IAM global-in-account, CloudWatch log groups regional with centralization); cross-account access as deliberate both-sides trust; and the vanished-resource trio: account → region → IAM permission — with the pop quiz, real-world picks and the where-does-it-live scope drill.

days.title: CI/CD and AWS Developer Tools
days.summary: Week 3, session 2 — exam-focused CLF-C02 Domain 3 notes: what CI/CD is and why it makes change easy: small frequent code changes integrated at least once a day (the exam cadence, matched by AWS’s whitepaper ‘at minimum once a day’) and the build-test-deploy functions automated so bugs are caught while small; AWS’s delivery-vs-deployment split (automated build/test/preparation plus a manual approval before production vs approval automated by pre-configured rules) with some teams delivering several times a day; the example workflow — local build and test, commit to the shared repository, then merge, build, re-test, package, and deploy automatically; the four developer tools mapped to their jobs — CodeCommit (a private Git repository in the cloud storing source, binaries, images and libraries, managing collaboration and version history; closed to new customers 2024-07-25 and reopened 2025-11-25 per the official docs history), CodeBuild (a fully managed build service compiling, testing, producing packages and Docker images from CodeCommit code), CodeDeploy (automated deployments to EC2, on-premises systems and Lambda — the docs add Amazon ECS with canary/linear/all-at-once traffic shifting — quick releases without downtime) and CodePipeline (the continuous-delivery service modeling, visualizing and automating every release step, triggered on every code change); and the CloudShell + CLI walkthrough end to end — the browser shell with the CLI preinstalled and preconfigured, aws --version, aws s3 mb with a globally unique name, aws s3 ls, echo >> file.txt, cat, aws s3 cp, aws s3 ls bucket, the help pager (examples at the very end, q exits) and the version-2 CLI Command Reference organized by service.

days.title: AWS Monitoring Fundamentals (CloudWatch)
days.summary: Week 3, day 2 — exam-focused notes (CloudWatch, CLF-C02 Domain 3): telemetry monitoring — automated collection of data from remote sources into a central location at predefined time increments — with CloudWatch as the central repository for metrics, home of alarms and rules that action other services; which services send metrics (compute: EC2, auto-scaling groups, ELB, Route 53 health checks, Lambda; storage and content delivery: EBS, Storage Gateway, CloudFront; database and analytics: DynamoDB tables, ElastiCache, RDS, Redshift, EMR; plus SNS, SQS, SWF); the metrics hierarchy of namespaces and dimensions with per-instance metric examples — and the docs extras (no default namespace, AWS/service naming convention, metrics live only in their Region and expire after 15 months); basic monitoring (default, free, every 5 minutes) vs detailed monitoring (certain resource types, charged, every 1 minute — enhanced monitoring on Beanstalk, request metrics on S3); the CloudWatch agent (downloadable package, wide OS support, wizard, in-guest memory and page file metrics the defaults miss, installed via CLI or Systems Manager with configure-once reuse); CloudWatch Logs — log events into streams into groups, Standard vs Infrequent Access log classes (Infrequent Access is renamed Essentials in today's docs, and a log group's class is locked at creation), Live Tail and anomaly detection as Standard-class features, metric filters translating logs into numeric metrics, vended vs custom logs, and the three ways to send logs (agent, CLI PutLogEvents command, PutLogEvents API); CloudWatch alarms with the three states (OK, In alarm, Insufficient data) and push notifications via SNS topics + email subscriptions, no custom code; closing with the full first-alarm walkthrough: a t3.micro EC2 instance loaded with the stress tool until CPUUtilization (threshold greater than 10% on a five-minute period) flips the alarm from Insufficient data to In alarm and the SNS email arrives — one out of the last one data point greater than the threshold of 10.

days.title: Asynchronous Messaging in AWS (SNS / SQS)
days.summary: Session 3 — an exam-focused groundwork page: every fact verified against live AWS documentation (Nov 3, 2026) via API-backed search and fetch, and every cited link curl-checked before publishing. Topic: asynchronous messaging in AWS — the doc definition of a message queue (a form of asynchronous service-to-service communication used in serverless and microservices architectures; messages are stored until processed and deleted), and the two primitives for decoupling. SQS: fully managed pull-based queuing — producers SendMessage, consumers ReceiveMessage, process, DeleteMessage; standard queues (the default) run nearly unlimited API calls per second with guaranteed at-least-once delivery (occasional duplicates — keep consumers idempotent or dedupe by message ID) and best-effort ordering; FIFO queues deliver exactly-once processing and strict ordering (name must end .fifo — the suffix counts toward the 80-character quota; high-throughput mode reaches 3,000 messages per second with batching or 300 per second per operation); verified numbers — max message size 1 MiB (1,048,576 bytes; the 256 KB figure is outdated), retention default 4 days, minimum 60 seconds, maximum 14 days (1,209,600 seconds); visibility timeout default 30 seconds, maximum 12 hours, zero releases a message to another consumer; short polling responds immediately but can return empty responses, long polling waits up to 20 seconds (fewer empty responses, lower cost); dead-letter queues via a redrive policy with maxReceiveCount. SNS: fully managed pub/sub push with topics as logical access points, spanning Application-to-Application and Application-to-Person messaging; subscriber endpoint types (Amazon SQS, Lambda, HTTP/S, Email, Mobile push, Mobile text/SMS, Amazon Data Firehose, service providers like Datadog, MongoDB and Splunk); HTTP(S), email and cross-account subscribers must confirm subscriptions (pending up to 30 days); filter policies are JSON objects on the subscription selecting which messages a subscriber receives, keyed on message attributes (timestamps, geospatial data, signatures, identifiers); raw message delivery strips SNS metadata for SQS subscribers; message size default 256 KiB with AWS whats-new (Sept 18, 2026) raising payloads up to 1 MiB — a 4x increase — via per-topic MaximumMessageSize; SNS FIFO topics pair with SQS FIFO queues for ordered, deduplicated delivery; the fan-out pattern — one topic delivering copies of each message to multiple SQS queues for independent, asynchronous processing — and the choosing rule: SQS for one-to-one buffering, SNS for one-to-many push, SNS-into-SQS fan-out when broadcast plus durable per-consumer buffers are both needed. Fresh 40 flashcards, 40 true/false (page-internal dedupe clean, zero overlap with today's earlier pages), pop quiz, real-world picks and an 8-row which-service drill (SQS / SNS / fan-out).

days.title: CloudWatch Events + EventBridge Scheduler (SNS/SQS patterns)
days.summary: An exam-focused groundwork page: every fact verified against live AWS documentation (Nov 9, 2026), all links GET-verified 200 before publishing. Topic: CloudWatch Events + EventBridge Scheduler and the practical SNS/SQS integration — today's bus lineup: a default bus automatically receiving AWS service state-change events (250+ services send them; S3 data-plane events once EventBridge is enabled on the bucket; alarm state-change events with guaranteed delivery — source aws.cloudwatch, detail-type CloudWatch Alarm State Change), Custom Event Bus - Classic since July 2019 (rules and targets: 300 rules per event bus, 5 targets per rule — not adjustable, 2,048-character event patterns, 100 buses per account; SQS standard/fair/FIFO queues with SqsParameters message groups, SNS topics, Lambda, Step Functions, SSM, API destinations; the input transformer with up to 100 JSONPath variables from the original event), and the new Custom Event Bus (September 2026: AWS RAM sharing where consumer accounts own their subscribers — one target per subscriber, 1–365-day bus retention, FIFO delivery within an event group, replay via a starting position, publish-time deduplication in a 5-minute window, PutRawEvents for Avro/Protobuf/raw bytes, JSONata transforms, universal targets calling any state-changing AWS API); event JSON anatomy (source, detail-type and detail required for PutEvents; the id UUID traces events through rules to targets); scheduled rules as legacy — six-field cron with ? in one of the two day fields, L/W/# wildcards, nothing faster than 1 minute, UTC — succeeded by EventBridge Scheduler (one-time at() schedules; cron/rate in any time zone with automatic DST; 60-second precision; flexible time windows dispersing invocations for reliability; retry policies of up to 185 attempts over up to 24 hours; SQS DLQs receiving a JSON dead-letter event; 10,000,000 schedules per Region; 14,000,000 invocations/month free then $1.00 per million); rule-target delivery retries by default 185 times over 24 hours with exponential backoff and jitter, then drops events unless a standard-SQS DLQ carries them with RULE_ARN/TARGET_ARN/ERROR_CODE attributes; and the industry-standard setups — alarm-state rules into SNS topics for humans, event rules into per-consumer SQS queues for durable pacing with their own DLQs, Scheduler into SQS/Lambda for timezoned jobs, SNS as the fan-out multiplier beyond the 5-target rule cap, FIFO event groups when order matters, and 64-KB-chunk event pricing pushing large payloads to S3 with pointer events.

days.title: AWS CloudFormation (Infrastructure as Code)
days.summary: An exam-focused groundwork page: every fact verified against live AWS documentation (Nov 9, 2026), all links GET-verified 200 before publishing. Topic: AWS CloudFormation — templates and stacks (a template describes your resources, the stack provisions them in dependency order and delete removes the whole set; JSON or YAML with only the Resources section required, at least one resource; authoring via template studio, a text editor, or the IaC generator that generates templates from resources not currently managed by CloudFormation; Git sync monitors a repository branch for template changes); intrinsic functions (Ref, Fn::GetAtt, Fn::Sub, Fn::Join, Fn::FindInMap, Fn::Select, Fn::If, Fn::ImportValue — usable only in resource properties, outputs, metadata, update policies and conditions) and pseudo parameters (AWS::Region, AWS::StackName, AWS::AccountId, AWS::Partition, AWS::NoValue removing a property inside Fn::If, and AWS::NotificationARNs as a list read with Fn::Select); the verified quota table (500 resources per template, 200 parameters, 200 outputs, 200 mappings, 255-character names, 51,200-byte template body in a request or 1 MB via an S3 object, 2,000 stacks per account and Region, 1,000 stack sets, 2,500 resources per single nested-hierarchy deployment, 60 dynamic references); stack creation with OnFailure — DO_NOTHING, ROLLBACK (the default) or DELETE, mutually exclusive with DisableRollback, with StackSets deployments overriding the default to DELETE — and termination protection off by default; change sets that preview proposed updates including which resources would be replaced or deleted and change nothing until executed (and which do not guarantee a successful update because runtime conditions can still fail — with pre-deployment validation catching syntax errors, name conflicts and quota limits; express mode applies operations as soon as configuration lands); the three update behaviors — no interruption (physical ID unchanged), some interruption, and replacement with a new physical ID where the replacement is created first, references are re-pointed and the old resource deleted (EC2 AvailabilityZone and RDS Port as the canonical examples; adding or removing such a property triggers replacement even if the value never changed); DeletionPolicy (default Delete — Retain for any resource, Snapshot for snapshot-capable ones like AWS::EC2::Volume, with AWS::RDS::DBCluster and DBInstance without DBClusterIdentifier defaulting to Snapshot; empty S3 buckets required for deletion to succeed) versus UpdateReplacePolicy (retain or snapshot the OLD physical instance, executed only when the update behavior is Replacement; retained resources keep billing and leave CloudFormation's scope); drift detection (actual versus expected configuration with changed or deleted properties counting, DRIFTED / in-sync / NOT_CHECKED statuses, whole-stack or per-resource checks, resolved with corrective action or an import operation); StackSets (one operation across many accounts and Regions from one template with per-stack parameter customization; administrator and target accounts with a trust relationship; self-managed permissions where you create the IAM roles versus service-managed where StackSets creates them and can auto-deploy to accounts added to the organization later; operation preferences for Region order, failure tolerance and concurrency; a StackSet is a regional resource); cross-stack references (Outputs with an Export name read by Fn::ImportValue, same account and Region); nested stacks (AWS::CloudFormation::Stack splitting a template into reusable pieces under a root stack), cfn-init (AWS::CloudFormation::Init in EC2 metadata — the helper script run from user data installs packages, writes files and enables/disables plus starts/stops services), and custom resources (AWS::CloudFormation::CustomResource or Custom::… with the one required property being the service token — Lambda or SNS — for resources not available as built-in types); plus modules in the registry and the documented best-practice list (organize stacks by lifecycle and ownership, manage all stack resources through CloudFormation, change sets before updates, stack policies, CloudTrail logging, code review and revision control, regular drift detection, never embedding credentials).

Day 13 — exam-focused notes (CLF-C02 Domain 4 · Billing, Pricing, and Support): pay-as-you-go economics and the shared cost responsibility — moving to the cloud trades fixed expense for variable, and unattended waste is billed anyway; TCO thinking with the Pricing Calculator (estimate + CSV export); compute purchasing options: On-Demand pay-per-second/no commitment, Reserved Instances up to 72% on 1–3-year commitments (all/partial/no upfront), Savings Plans committing to dollars-per-hour across eligible families, Spot up to 90% interruptible with a two-minute warning for batch/flexible jobs; spend-lean compute habits — right-sizing, Auto Scaling to demand, dev/test environments off nights and weekends, Compute Optimizer ML recommendations; storage cost levers — S3 storage classes (Standard vs Infrequent Access vs Glacier tiers) with per-GB retrieval fees on archive classes, lifecycle policies transitioning to IA, expiring stale versions and aborting incomplete multipart uploads; data transfer rulebook — inbound free, outbound about ten cents/GB with the first 100 GB/month per account free (today's docs), cross-AZ and cross-region movement billed, CloudFront egress cheaper than EC2/S3; monitoring and predicting costs — AWS Budgets (actual + forecasted alerts by email or SNS; a $10 budget's three default alerts: actual 85% = $8.50, actual 100%, forecasted 100%, firing only after email verification), Cost Explorer (13 months history, 12-month forecast), and the most-detailed Cost and Usage Report (delivered daily to S3 in zipped files split at up to 500 MB, queried with Athena); multi-account billing — consolidated billing in AWS Organizations (one payer bill, pooled volume discounts, RI/Savings Plans sharing, member accounts track their own costs) plus Billing Conductor's custom billing views for resellers; tagging and resource groups with cost allocation tags activated in the Billing console; Trusted Advisor cost checks (idle load balancers, unattached EBS volumes; seven core checks on Basic support per today's docs); support — the legacy tiers (Developer $29, Business $100, Enterprise On-Ramp $5,500, Enterprise $15,000) flagged against today's docs: Developer/Business/Enterprise On-Ramp discontinued January 1, 2027, current lineup Basic (free), Business Support+ from $29/month (AI-powered, 24/7), Enterprise Support with designated TAM + 15-minute responses at a $5,000 minimum (was $15,000), plus AWS Unified Operations; beyond tickets — re:Post, Knowledge Center, AWS Partner Network, Managed Services, AWS Activate credits; exam framing: billing, pricing, and support is the smallest CLF-C02 domain at 12% of scored content.
days.title: Pricing, Billing, and Support (Cost Management)

days.summary: Session 2 — an exam-focused groundwork page: every fact verified against live AWS documentation (Nov 9, 2026) via API-backed search and fetch, and every cited link curl-checked before publishing. Topic: security and compliance fundamentals — the shared responsibility model and how duties shift between EC2, RDS, and Lambda; the account root user and the short list only root can do (close the account, change the account email/contact info, restore IAM user permissions), MFA and no root access keys; least privilege with users, groups, and roles holding temporary credentials, policy evaluation where an explicit deny beats every allow and no allow means implicit deny, access keys vs passwords, and IAM Identity Center (formerly AWS Single Sign-On) for federation; encryption in transit (TLS) and at rest (KMS keys, yearly default rotation for customer-managed symmetric keys) with S3 encrypting every new upload by default (SSE-S3); the audit trail (CloudTrail: who did what from which IP, 90-day console event history, trails for more) vs the configuration trail (AWS Config: settings history evaluated against compliance rules); the detection lineup — GuardDuty (ML over CloudTrail management events, VPC flow logs, and DNS logs), Inspector (vulnerability scans for EC2, ECR images, and Lambda), Macie (PII and sensitive-data discovery in S3), Security Hub (consolidated findings against security standards); compliance self-service from AWS Artifact (SOC/PCI-style reports and agreements) with Audit Manager collecting evidence, and requirements varying by geography and industry; edge defense with AWS WAF (layer-7 managed rule groups on a web ACL) and AWS Shield (Standard free and automatic, Advanced paid), plus Secrets Manager rotation and Parameter Store SecureString; and the exam framing: Domain 2 is 30% of scored content, second only to Domain 3.
